title: A narrow hold as the MPC weighs a spring fall in inflation
summary: The Monetary Policy Committee kept Bank Rate at 3.75% by five votes to four. All four dissenters wanted a quarter-point cut. The Committee judged that further reductions were likely, having already cut 150 basis points since August 2024. For sterling rates, the important distinction within the majority was between members who wanted a longer period of restraint and those who could envisage easing once they saw how lower inflation affected wage settlements. The expected return to 2% did not settle the timing for either group. Governor Andrew Bailey explicitly left open his vote at each subsequent meeting (summary and minutes, paragraphs 11 and 16–20).

Annual CPI inflation had fallen from 3.8% in September to 3.4% in December. The MPC expected energy prices, including the effect of measures in the 2025 Budget, to bring inflation close to target from April. This represented a sizeable revision relative to the November forecast, with less new information since the December meeting. The harder question was how long the effects would last. Some members thought cheaper energy and food could quickly temper household expectations and pay demands. The Bank’s Agents’ survey pointed to settlements of 3.4% in 2026. Other forward indicators of pay remained firmer, and both wages and services prices were still rising faster than members considered consistent with the target (paragraphs 3–6).

Employment and productivity gave conflicting signals about domestic price pressure. Underlying output growth was running below estimated potential, unemployment had risen just above 5% and the staff projection incorporated more spare capacity than in November. Persistently high household saving could depress consumption and employment further. Yet vacancies had begun to rise, bank lending and broad money growth had strengthened a little, and weak productivity could sustain labour costs even as pay growth slowed. A smaller productive capacity would leave less room for demand to recover without generating inflation. Members attributed much of their reassessment to staff analysis rather than the latest releases (paragraphs 7–10).

Among the five who voted to hold, Bailey and Catherine Mann placed greater weight on weak activity. Mann nevertheless saw a risk that cutting on the strength of a temporary drop in headline inflation could raise term premia. Megan Greene, Clare Lombardelli and Huw Pill favoured a longer period of restraint. The four dissenters saw greater costs in waiting, particularly if weakening demand eventually forced much sharper cuts. Alan Taylor pointed to successive forecast revisions showing lower inflation and more spare capacity even as the interest rate path assumed in those forecasts had moved down. He read that combination as evidence against the persistence scenario (paragraphs 13 and 16–20).

The conditioning market curve eased slightly during 2026 before rising towards 3.75% in 2029. The median participant in the Bank’s survey expected Bank Rate eventually to settle at 3.25%. The MPC observed that the upward curve was raising financing costs for households and firms, while acknowledging that forward rates could contain more than expected future policy. The survey therefore offers a comparison of beliefs, not a direct estimate of the market’s pricing error. The minutes give neither announcement-window returns nor an estimate of the term premium (paragraph 14 and footnote 1).

questions.question: Will the expected fall in headline inflation change wage settlements soon enough to bring forward a cut?
questions.detail: The Agents’ survey pointed to lower settlements, but Bailey identified uncertainty about when firms would respond. An annual average can conceal contracts fixed before the energy-price adjustment. The timing matters for exposure to the next few MPC meetings. Start with Boxes A and B of the February Monetary Policy Report, then compare dated settlement rounds and household expectations with the survey evidence available at the meeting.

questions.question: How much of the shortfall in activity reflects weak demand rather than weaker productive capacity?
questions.detail: The central projection allowed more slack, while Greene questioned the assumed productivity recovery. The same growth outturn could therefore justify different policy rates. Inspect the smaller-output-gap sensitivity in section 3.2 and the productivity analysis in Box C of the February Report. Check real-time output per hour, unit labour costs, vacancies and hours worked for evidence that would distinguish the two accounts.

questions.question: How much of the upward forward curve was compensation for risk, and how much reached borrowers?
questions.detail: The MPC identified a financing channel but did not quantify its components. This affects whether an investor seeking exposure to expected easing would also assume substantial longer-dated rate risk. Compare the dated Market Participants Survey with maturity-matched sterling overnight-indexed swap forwards, then examine fixed mortgage quotes and corporate borrowing rates. Allow for risk premia, credit spreads and the composition of survey responses when interpreting the differences.

limitation: The Bank’s current text incorporates a 24 February wording correction to paragraph 14 about the survey median. The 3.25% figure is unchanged. The accompanying Monetary Policy Report is a separate publication.
